answers.answer: DNS resolves api.notes.example, not /notes/42. The stub is the client's local helper and asks the recursive resolver to find the answer. With empty caches the recursive resolver asks root, follows its .example referral, then the .example referral to the notes.example authority. Delegation assigns a child zone's responsibility to authoritative servers; a zone is a managed portion of names, and a referral points toward its authority rather than supplying the final host address. The authority supplies api's CNAME to edge.notes.example. A CNAME contains another name, so the resolver still needs edge's A (IPv4) or AAAA (IPv6) data, supplied with the alias or obtained through another lookup here. The recursive result returns to the stub; the client chooses a reachable address family, connects, verifies HTTPS for api.notes.example and sends the HTTP request for /notes/42. Later, cached answers or delegations can shorten discovery; alias and target records cache separately, and an existing connection can avoid a new lookup. An address establishes no application-health guarantee.

evidence.quote: DNS resolves the hostname, not the URL path, and does not carry the later HTTP exchange.

The stub resolver is the client's local lookup helper. It asks a recursive resolver to obtain an answer on its behalf. An authoritative server supplies records for a zone, a managed portion of DNS names.
Delegation assigns responsibility for a child zone to its authoritative servers. A referral points the resolver toward them; it is not the final host address.

The recursive resolver returns the result to the stub. Cached answers can avoid authority visits, and cached delegations can let it start closer to the answer. The stub need not perform each visit itself.
An A record supplies an IPv4 address; an AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address. A client uses an address family it can reach.
A CNAME record is a name alias. Resolving it follows the target name to obtain A or AAAA data, possibly already cached or returned with the alias. Otherwise another lookup is needed.
Alias and target records can be cached separately. The alias creates a dependency on the target's DNS data, even when both names have the same operator.
An address answer does not establish that the application is healthy. A usable cached address or an existing connection can avoid a fresh lookup.
The client must still verify the certificate for the hostname it requested, api.example.test, even if DNS followed an alias to edge.example.test.

answers.answer: TTL limits ordinary cached-answer reuse in seconds and ages independently in each cache. The 3600-second answer cached at 11:59 can remain ordinarily usable until 12:59, so lowering the authoritative TTL at noon does not force a refresh by 12:01. For a planned move, lower the TTL while retaining the old address, allow the previous 3600-second lifetime to age out, then switch. Keep the old destination usable through the transition, observing traffic, errors and existing connections at both destinations before retiring it. The lesson supplies no fixed universally safe retirement deadline: connections do not migrate and some resolvers can serve expired data after refresh failures. Short TTLs increase refresh queries and dependence on working DNS. Independent cache ages and connection lifetimes prevent a worldwide simultaneous cutover.

evidence.quote: TTL, or time to live, limits ordinary cache reuse in seconds. Each cache ages the TTL it received; it is not a worldwide update timer.
Its existing entry can still be ordinarily usable until 10:05; the edit does not rewrite that entry.

For a planned move, lower TTL first, allow the previous longer TTL to age out, then switch. Keep the old destination usable through the transition while monitoring traffic, errors and existing connections at both destinations. DNS edits do not migrate open connections.

Shorter TTLs mean more refresh queries and more frequent dependence on working DNS. Independent caches and connection lifetimes prevent a simultaneous cutover. Some resolvers can even serve expired data when refreshing fails, so TTL is not a hard global recovery deadline.

answers.answer: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence. The earlier NXDOMAIN has its own cache lifetime, and publishing an A record does not notify that cache; its new 30-second positive TTL therefore does not clear the earlier result. NXDOMAIN says the queried name does not exist, though this cached answer may predate creation. NODATA for AAAA says the name exists but lacks that requested type; it does not imply no A record or no name. SERVFAIL says resolution could not be completed, not that the name is absent. Such failures may also be cached to avoid repeatedly querying failing servers. Inspect the requested name, record type and returned status to distinguish these cases; the scenario does not supply the negative entry's remaining lifetime.

evidence.quote: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence. NXDOMAIN says the queried name does not exist. NODATA means the name exists but has no record of the requested type: no AAAA record does not imply no A record or no name.
Adding its A record does not notify that cache. The negative answer has its own cache lifetime; the new positive record's TTL does not clear it.

SERVFAIL means resolution could not be completed, for example because the resolver could not obtain usable answers. It is not proof that the name does not exist. Resolution failures may also be cached to avoid repeatedly hammering failing DNS servers.
Check the requested name, record type and returned status before changing records.

answers.answer: Steering selects destinations returned in DNS answers; failover changes that selection after failure. A separate health check and policy, or an operator, must detect east's failure and change answers because ordinary records do not detect application health. Equal shares of DNS answers do not imply equal HTTP-request shares: one recursive cache may serve many clients, and a client can reuse an address or connection for many requests. Removing east affects future discovery, while cached clients may still try east and existing connections do not move to west. West must be reachable, healthy and have enough spare capacity for redirected work. Health checks sample health, and DNS neither creates capacity nor guarantees instant or universal request success.

evidence.quote: DNS traffic steering selects destinations returned in answers. Failover changes the selected destination after failure. For east and west endpoints, a separate health check and policy, or an operator, must detect east's failure and change answers. Ordinary DNS records do not detect application health themselves.

Returning east for half of lookups does not guarantee half of HTTP requests reach east. A shared recursive resolver can reuse one answer for many clients, and each client may send many requests using that address or connection.

After east is removed from new answers, cached clients can still try it. Existing connections do not migrate to west just because DNS changed. DNS is not choosing a destination again for every HTTP request.

West must be reachable, healthy and have enough spare capacity for redirected work. A health signal is a sample, not a promise that every request succeeds; DNS changes do not create capacity or guarantee instant recovery.

answers.answer: Open connections can continue without another lookup, and a usable cached address can allow connection despite a DNS outage. New users needing uncached discovery depend on a reachable recursive resolver, functioning delegation and answering authorities. Start at the affected client's recursive resolver: check exact name, type, answer or error and remaining TTL; compare authoritative records and parent delegation when wrong or failing. A new authoritative address alongside an old cached address suggests cache aging rather than an automatic edit. After obtaining the expected address, check connection, HTTPS and application results separately. HTTP 500 means an HTTP service responded with an error, so it alone is not evidence of DNS failure. The scenario does not establish the exact cause of either failure. Reachable alternate resolvers and authoritative servers help individual-server failures but cannot repair shared wrong records, broken delegation or a failed Notes application.

evidence.quote: During a DNS outage, a client with a usable cached address may still connect, and an open connection may keep working without a lookup. Fresh uncached lookups need a reachable recursive resolver, working delegation and authoritative servers that can answer.

Start with the client's recursive resolver: inspect the queried name and type, its answer or error, and remaining TTL. Compare authoritative data and parent delegation when results are wrong or failing. An authoritative new address beside a cached old one suggests a cache-age question, not an automatic need for another edit.

Once the expected address is obtained, inspect connection, HTTPS and application results separately. HTTP 500 means an HTTP service responded with an error; it is not by itself a DNS lookup failure. Successful DNS does not prove the application works.

Reachable alternate resolvers and authoritative servers reduce individual server failures. They cannot fix a shared wrong record, broken delegation or a failed application. Several DNS servers with the same bad configuration can return the same wrong result.

answers.answer: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data. A validating resolver checks a chain of trust beginning at a configured trusted key, with each trusted signing key vouching for the next link. Successful validation establishes signed DNS data's origin and integrity, including detection of alteration; it does not validate the application. It neither hides the query nor proves Notes healthy or available. HTTPS certificate checks remain necessary: HTTPS authenticates the endpoint through certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange. The client verifies api.notes.example, the hostname requested, even if DNS follows an alias to a different name.

evidence.quote: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data. A validating resolver checks those signatures through a chain of trust: each trusted signing key vouches for the next link, starting at a configured trusted key. Successful validation establishes the signed data's origin and integrity, meaning it has not been altered without detection.
That validates DNS data, not the application. DNSSEC does not encrypt the query, certify service health or guarantee availability.

HTTPS separately authenticates the endpoint through certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange. The client must still verify the certificate for the hostname it requested, api.example.test, even if DNS followed an alias to edge.example.test.
A valid DNSSEC answer does not remove HTTPS certificate checks.
